Newborn Care

Understanding a retained placenta

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

The placenta still needs to be delivered after the baby is born. If it does not come away, or pieces remain inside the uterus, the birth team needs to assess the cause and prevent or treat bleeding and infection.

The placenta is delivered after the baby

Birth is usually described in three stages: the cervix opens, the baby is born, and then the placenta and membranes are delivered. During this third stage, the uterus contracts so the placenta separates and can pass out. Contraction also helps close the blood vessels at the attachment site.

A retained placenta means that the placenta has not been delivered when expected, or that tissue remains inside afterward. It can interfere with normal uterine contraction and cause serious bleeding or infection. It needs assessment by the birth team; it is not something to manage by pulling on the cord yourself.

When is the third stage considered prolonged?

The threshold depends on how the third stage is managed and on local guidance. NICE uses 30 minutes with active management, which includes a medicine to help the uterus contract, and 60 minutes with physiological management, where the placenta is initially allowed to deliver without that treatment.

These timings help clinicians organise care; they are not a safe waiting period when bleeding is heavy or someone is unwell. Treatment may be needed earlier. If the placenta has not delivered during physiological management, the team may recommend changing to active management. Ask what is happening and what the next step will be.

Three different mechanisms can be involved

Sometimes the uterus does not contract effectively enough for the placenta to separate. This is often called placenta adherens. In another situation, the placenta has separated but is trapped behind a cervix that has begun to close.

Placenta accreta spectrum is different: placental tissue is abnormally attached to, or grows into, the uterine muscle. Trying to force it away can cause major haemorrhage. These mechanisms can require different decisions, so “retained” describes the problem but does not by itself establish the cause or the safest removal method.

Who is more likely to experience it?

A previous retained placenta is relevant to a future birth plan. Preterm birth, prior uterine surgery or procedures, uterine structural differences and some placental conditions may also increase the likelihood. A retained placenta can still occur without a known risk factor.

Research has examined age, a prolonged first or second stage of labour and pregnancies ending in stillbirth, among other factors. These associations do not create a universal age-over-30 rule or a single gestational-week cutoff. The team considers the whole history, including bleeding and accreta risks. Tell them about previous difficult placental delivery or major bleeding, even if the last birth was elsewhere.

What the team checks immediately after birth

If the placenta has not delivered, staff assess blood loss, pulse, blood pressure, uterine contraction and your overall condition. They also consider whether it has separated or may be abnormally attached. Intravenous access allows fluids, medicines or blood products to be given quickly if needed.

After delivery, the placenta and membranes are examined for completeness. Missing pieces may suggest retained tissue, although inspection cannot exclude every small fragment. Further examination or ultrasound may be considered when the findings or symptoms raise concern. A scan is interpreted alongside the clinical picture, rather than treated as a perfect yes-or-no answer.

Symptoms can appear later as well

Small pieces of tissue can cause problems after the main placenta has been delivered, including after discharge. Increasing or persistent heavy bleeding, fever, unpleasant-smelling discharge and worsening pelvic or abdominal pain need prompt medical advice. Symptoms do not have to begin on the first day.

Normal postpartum bleeding should generally lessen over time. Seek immediate care for bleeding that soaks a pad in an hour, very large clots, severe pain, a temperature of 38°C or higher, or feeling markedly unwell. Fainting, breathlessness, chest pain or uncontrolled bleeding needs emergency help. Tell the clinician when you gave birth and whether any placental problem was recorded.

Supportive steps and the role of medicines

When the situation is stable, the team may help you empty your bladder or change position. Breastfeeding or skin-to-skin contact may support normal hormone release and uterine contraction if you and the baby are well enough. These measures do not replace treatment for significant retention or bleeding, and difficulty breastfeeding is not a reason to blame yourself.

Uterotonic medicines help the uterus contract and are important when bleeding is excessive. Additional intravenous uterotonics are not a routine solution for every retained placenta without bleeding. A medicine that relaxes the uterus or cervix may sometimes be considered in a selected situation, but it is not an established home remedy or a guaranteed alternative to removal.

Manual removal requires anaesthesia

If removal is needed and appropriate, a clinician may remove the placenta through the vagina by hand, usually in a theatre setting. The procedure needs anaesthesia; it should not be performed as an unanaesthetised uterine exploration. The anaesthetic approach depends on urgency, your condition and whether a suitable epidural is already in place.

The team should explain the reason for the procedure and obtain consent as circumstances allow. Let staff know if pain relief is inadequate. After removal they reassess bleeding and uterine tone. WHO recommends preventive antibiotics for manual removal because of infection concerns, while acknowledging uncertainty in the direct evidence; the drug choice depends on allergies and local practice.

When a procedure or more urgent surgery is necessary

If tissue remains, removal is incomplete or bleeding continues, a procedure to empty the uterus may be needed. The exact technique depends on the situation and specialist assessment. Significant bleeding may also require transfusion, medicines and other measures to control haemorrhage.

There is no rule that every gentle measure must be tried before surgery. In an emergency, delaying effective treatment can be dangerous. If accreta spectrum is suspected, forceful separation may be avoided and senior specialist help is required. Occasionally major surgery, including hysterectomy, is needed to control life-threatening bleeding. This is a possible escalation, not the expected outcome of every retained placenta.

Can it be prevented?

Active management of the third stage reduces the risk of heavy bleeding after birth. It usually includes a uterotonic and, when appropriate, controlled cord traction by a trained clinician after signs of separation. The choice between active and physiological management can be discussed before birth and revisited if circumstances change.

No method guarantees that the placenta will deliver normally. Pulling the cord, pushing on the uterus yourself or relying on home massage is unsafe. Clinical uterine massage may be part of treating poor contraction or haemorrhage; it is not a self-care technique that prevents retained placenta. A prior history helps the team prepare staff, anaesthesia and blood-loss management.

Recovery after treatment

Recovery depends on how much bleeding occurred, whether infection developed and what treatment was needed. Follow-up may include checking for anaemia, taking prescribed iron or antibiotics and reviewing ongoing bleeding or pain. Ask for written instructions about symptoms, medicines and whom to contact after discharge.

A difficult third stage can interrupt the first hours with the baby and feel frightening. Practical help with feeding, rest and daily tasks may be useful, and you can request a birth debrief to understand the sequence of events. Persistent dizziness, worsening symptoms or feeling emotionally overwhelmed deserve support rather than being dismissed as inevitable after childbirth.

What it means for a future pregnancy

Having had a retained placenta increases the chance of it happening again, but recurrence is not inevitable. Keep a copy of the birth summary if possible. Whether the issue was poor separation, trapped tissue or accreta matters for future planning.

Discuss the history early in the next pregnancy so the team can consider the appropriate birth setting and any extra assessment. Ask whether the placenta was complete, whether pathology changed the diagnosis and whether follow-up is outstanding. Most people recover after timely treatment, but the individual account is more informative than reassurance based only on the label.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

A prolonged third stage has different thresholds with active and physiological management.

Heavy bleeding or instability overrides a clock-based waiting period; manual removal requires anaesthesia.

How BeMama can help

Keep the birth summary and ask for a clear explanation of the cause, treatment and follow-up plan.

When to seek help

After birth, heavy bleeding, fever, severe pain or foul-smelling discharge needs immediate advice. Uncontrolled bleeding, fainting, chest pain or breathing difficulty requires emergency care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The placenta can fail to separate, become trapped or be abnormally attached.
  • Bleeding and clinical condition determine urgency.
  • Symptoms from retained fragments may occur after discharge.
  • Manual removal requires anaesthesia and infection precautions.
  • Record the history so future birth care can be prepared.

Frequently asked questions

Is 30 minutes always the definition?

No. NICE uses 30 minutes after active management and 60 minutes after physiological management. Other guidance may vary. Heavy bleeding or an unwell patient needs earlier action regardless of elapsed time.

Can a placenta be retained even after most of it comes out?

Yes. Small fragments can remain and cause delayed bleeding or infection. Worsening symptoms after discharge still need assessment even if the placenta seemed to have delivered.

Is retained placenta the same as placenta accreta?

No. Accreta spectrum is one possible cause involving abnormal attachment or invasion. Poor uterine contraction or tissue trapped behind the cervix can also cause retention.

Can I breastfeed to make it come out?

Feeding may support normal contractions when it is safe and comfortable, but it is not treatment for an emergency. Follow the birth team’s plan and do not delay needed removal or bleeding control.

Should manual removal be done without an anaesthetic?

No. Uterine exploration and manual removal require anaesthesia. Tell staff if pain relief is inadequate, and ask for an explanation of the plan.

Why might I be given antibiotics?

Manual removal involves entering the uterus. WHO recommends preventive antibiotics because of infection risk, although direct evidence of benefit is uncertain. The team chooses a suitable medicine using your allergy history and local guidance.

Does every retained placenta require major surgery?

No. Many are managed with appropriate removal and bleeding control. Further surgery is sometimes necessary for persistent tissue, severe bleeding or abnormal attachment; the team should explain why.

Can symptoms start several days after birth?

Yes. Retained fragments or infection can cause later bleeding, fever, pain or offensive discharge. Seek advice promptly rather than waiting for a routine postnatal appointment.

Does being over 30 mean this will happen?

No. Age alone is not a diagnosis or a reliable prediction. Previous retained placenta, uterine procedures and the current birth circumstances are among the factors clinicians consider.

Will it happen again at my next birth?

It is more likely after a previous retained placenta, but not inevitable. Share the earlier birth record so the team can plan the setting and response to any bleeding or delivery difficulty.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
